title: Lebaran — going home, and asking forgiveness
goal: Take part in Lebaran like a guest who knows what is going on: the journey home, the greetings, the food, the visiting. Along the way, master the small prefix *se-*, which gives you "one", "the same", "every" and "as … as possible".
bekal: understand and use the Lebaran vocabulary: *mudik*, *cuti bersama*, *sungkem*, *halalbihalal*, *Mohon maaf lahir dan batin*
link events in time with *sebelum*, *sesudah*, *selama*, *sehabis*, *sepulang*, *sesampainya* and say *secepatnya*

notes: **Mudik** is the great annual trip home — from the city back to the *kampung* or *udik* (the countryside), which is where the word comes from. Tens of millions of people do it in the same few days, which is why the news talks about *arus mudik* (the outward flow) and, a week later, *arus balik* (the return flow). Bayu's parents live only an hour away, but it is still *mudik*: the word is about going back to where your family is, not about distance.

**Cuti bersama** — literally "leave together" — is the government's extra block of days off stuck onto the official holiday, so that the whole country can travel at once. Offices close, and anyone who has to work that week will tell you about it.

**Salat Id and sungkem.** *Salat Id* is the special morning prayer on the first day of Lebaran, held in mosques, fields and closed-off streets. Afterwards, in Javanese families, children kneel before their parents and grandparents, kiss their hand and ask forgiveness: that is *sungkem*, and the ritual is *sungkeman*. It is often the most emotional moment of the whole year.

**Kedengarannya** — "it sounds". It is *dengar* (hear) wrapped in *ke-…-an* plus *-nya*, and it has a twin, *kelihatannya* ("it looks", from *lihat*). Both are used exactly like the English: *Kedengarannya enak* (sounds nice), *Kelihatannya capek* (you look tired).

**Ibuku yang minta** — "it's my mother who asked". Putting *yang* before the verb puts the spotlight on the person before it, like an English cleft sentence (Unit 10 showed you *yang* describing things; here it is picking out the one who did it). The *lho* adds "you might not expect this, but…".

**Nggak usah repot-repot** — "don't go to any trouble" — is what every host says, and nobody takes it literally. Arriving empty-handed at a Lebaran visit is not done; a tin of *nastar* (pineapple tarts) or *kastengel* (cheese sticks) is the classic gift. 💬 The baku version is *Tidak usah repot-repot*.

grammars.title: Se- = "one" and "the same"
body: Glued to a measure word, *se-* is simply "one": it replaces *satu* and is what people really say. Glued to a place or a group, it means "sharing the same".
after: *Satu jam* is not wrong — it is what you say when you are counting carefully ("one hour, not two"). In ordinary speech *sejam, seminggu, sebulan, setahun* are the default, just as English says "an hour" rather than "one hour".

⚠️ You already know several words that are *se-* in disguise: *sedikit* (a little), *sebentar* (a moment), *seratus, seribu, sejuta* (Unit 18 comes back to those). Once you see the pattern, a lot of vocabulary collapses into one rule.

grammars.title: Se- for time: before, after, during, every
body: Four of the most useful time words in the language are also *se-* words. They work either before a noun or before a whole clause, with no extra "that" or "-ing".
after: The clause after *sebelum* often has no subject at all when it is obvious: *Sebelum makan, cuci tangan dulu* (wash your hands before you eat). *Tiap* is the short, spoken version of *setiap*: *tiap hari, tiap malam*.
⚠️ *Selama* is "for" with a stretch of time, never "for" as in "for you": *selama seminggu* (for a week), but *untuk kamu* (for you). English uses one word for both jobs; Indonesian does not.

notes: **Mohon maaf lahir dan batin** is THE Lebaran sentence: "I beg forgiveness, outwardly and inwardly" — for anything I have done and anything I have thought. The reply is *Sama-sama* or *Maaf lahir batin juga*. You say it to everyone, including people you have never wronged, including your boss, including the person selling you *ketupat*.

**Halalbihalal** is the Lebaran gathering where people meet to forgive one another: families, neighbourhoods and offices all hold one in the weeks after Lebaran. The word is Arabic-flavoured but was coined in Indonesia; do not expect Arabic speakers to know it.

**Selamat Idulfitri** — KBBI spells it as one word, *Idulfitri*. On cards and messages you will also see *Minal aidin wal faizin*, which many Indonesians believe means "forgive me". It does not — it is Arabic for roughly "may we be among those who return and triumph" — which is why it is nearly always followed by *mohon maaf lahir dan batin*.

**Monggo** and **matur nuwun** are Javanese: "please, go ahead" and "thank you". In Central Java a guest who uses them earns instant goodwill. *Monggo* is the gesture word — it accompanies an open palm pointing at the food, the chair, the door. The standard Indonesian equivalents are *silakan* and *terima kasih*.

**Dimakan dulu** — "be eaten first" — is how hosts offer food. The passive (Unit 4) makes the offer about the food, not about you, which feels more polite than a command. *Diminum, Mbak* (please drink) works the same way. The polite answer is to take at least something.

**Halah, kamu itu** — "oh, you" — is a mother dismissing her son's flattery with a smile. *Halah* is a Javanese-flavoured exclamation of "oh, come off it". It is affectionate here; said with a frown, it is not.

grammars.title: Se- + verb: "as soon as, once, upon"
body: *Se-* on a verb or a movement word gives a compact time clause: "upon doing X", "once X is done". Adding *-nya* makes it slightly more formal and more written.
after: The pattern *se- + adjective + -nya* means "as … as possible": *secepatnya* (as fast as possible), *sebisanya* (as best you can), *setidaknya* (at least). It is formal enough for an email to Mbak Nur and ordinary enough for a WhatsApp message.
💬 *Sekali* after an adjective is "very" (*enak sekali*); in front of a verb it is "once" (*sekali coba*). Position tells you which one you have.

blocks.text: Lebaran (*Idulfitri* in formal writing) marks the end of the fasting month. It is two official days, a week of *cuti bersama*, and in practice a month of visits, food and forgiveness. These are the words you will hear everywhere in that season.

blocks.title: A Lebaran message you can send
items: *Selamat Hari Raya Idulfitri. Mohon maaf lahir dan batin.* — the safe, correct message for anyone.
*Saya sekeluarga mengucapkan Selamat Idulfitri. Mohon maaf atas segala kesalahan.* — formal, for colleagues and your RT.
💬 *Met Lebaran, ya! Maafin semua salahku.* — to friends. *Maafin* is Jakarta *-in* for *maafkan* (Unit 19).

blocks.text: Everything in this unit comes down to four jobs of one prefix. When you meet a new *se-* word, ask which of the four it is doing; nine times out of ten the meaning falls out.
